data.title: The Peshiṭta and Syro-Hexapla Translations of Amos 1:3–2:16
data.abstractNote: The Peshitta and Syro-Hexapla are two translations of the Old Testament into Syriac. The Peshitta is a translation From the Hebrew, received by a Syriac-speaking Jewish or Christian Community in the 1st or 2nd Century CE. The Syro-Hexapla is a translation from the Greek, made for a Christian community in the 7th Century CE. This dissertation determines specific translation techniques used by the respective translators in Amos 1:3-2:16. An analysis of these translation techniques reveals certain aspects of the communities that receive the translations. While previous scholarship has addressed translation techniques in the Dodekapropheton of the Peshitta (of which the section Amos 1:3-2:16 is a part), this study is the first to address the translation techniques used by the Syro-Hexapla in any part of the Dodekapropheton. Through text criticism the respective Vorlage of the translations are determined. A detailed evaluation of semantics (grammar and vocabulary) is used to extract the translation techniques employed. Several conclusions are reached through text critical evaluation. The Vorlage of the Peshitta is identical to the consonantal text as found in the Masoretic Text, while the Vorlage of the Syro-Hexapla is based on the Old Greek. Semantic analysis shows that a dynamic equivalent translation technique is employed by the Peshitta's translator. This translator focuses on a clear communication of the message to the receptor audience, using the Septuagint or Jewish interpretation traditions when the Hebrew text is unclear or ambivalent. The translator of the Syro-Hexapla uses a formal equivalent translation technique, concentrating on an accurate rendering of the Greek text, not consciously seeking help from other translations or versions. The methodology employed in this dissertation proves effective in expanding and refining the findings of other scholars of the same material in the Peshitta. Applying the identical methodology to a thus far untouched study of the translation technique of the Syro-Hexapla's Dodekapropheton provides an impetus to continued work in this area.

data.title: Church–Imperial Power Relationship in the Persian Empire of the 5th Century: The Role of Politics in the Reception of the First Ecumenical Council
data.abstractNote: In the context of Constantine the Great’s reign and his influence on Christian life in the Byzantine Empire, it is of great interest to observe the reception of the First Ecumenical Council in the Eastern Syriac Church – the Council of Seleucia (410). This historical event is a suggestive example of the relationship between a non-Christian emperor and the Church outside the Byzantine Empire, and between the Persian and the Byzantine Empire as well. We will first dwell on the participation of the Eastern-Syriac leaders to the First Council of Nicaea, and then we will focus on the Council of Seleucia – its religious and political context, the implication of the secular power in its organisation, and its paradigmatic role for today state-Church relationship.

data.title: The Theophany of “the Back” of God in the Cave (Exodus 33) according to Isaac of Niniveh in Reference with “The Life of Moses” by St. Gregory of Nyssa
data.abstractNote: Among the East Syriac authors, Isaac of Nineveh occupies a prominent place – his works had almost an universal spreading in the entire Christian world. The originality of this author’s theological vision comes out of its synthetic character: between the Syriac and the Greek theological school, first one much more biblical, while the latter more philosophically oriented. This paper deals with what theology calls the “vision of God”, in particular the interpretation of the vision Moses had in the cleft of the rock (Ex. 33), according to Isaac of Niniveh and in reference with Gregory of Nyssa’s perspective and his mystical commentary on this biblical extract (“The Life of Moses”). Firstly, we will place the two authors in a historical, geographical and theological context, and then we will focus on the mystical interpretations they give to Moses’ third vision on the Sinai Mountain (Ex. 33,18-23). Last section will be dedicated to some conclusions vis-à-vis the methodological approaches proposed by the two authors, that will evidently come out from the research.

data.title: Academic Theology and Monastic Theology – Two Contrasting Approaches in the East Syriac Community between the 6th to 7th Century
data.abstractNote: By the end of the 6th century and the 7th century the life of the East Syriac community is characterized by a complexity of dogmatic controversies and conflicts of authority that shaped a specific mystical itinerary. There are three constitutive elements during this period: the school of Nisibis, the monastics and the institutional Church. Not all the time the three institutions cooperated well because of their different theological approaches and occasional internal disputes. This idea can be synthetized in what we might call the relation between the academic theology and the monastic spirituality. In this paper I will analyse some representative moments and characters for this period so that to picture the complexity of the ecclesiastical (theological, spiritual and liturgical) life in the East Syriac Church, in a difficult and decisive historical time, and yet a time of flourishing of religious literature.

data.title: Joseph Hazzaya and the Spiritual Itinerary
data.abstractNote: Joseph Hazzaya is one of the most well-known East Syriac mystics and a prolific writer, belonging to the same spiritual and theological family together with Isaac of Nineveh, Simon of Taibuteh and John Dalyatha. His name is also mentioned in the Christological debate of 786-787 in the East Syriac Church, during the time of Patriarch Timothy I, next to John the Solitary and John Dalyatha. The first chapter of this paper is dedicated to his theological biography, as revealing an important historical meeting between a scholastic-dogmatic theology and a spiritual-monastic perspective. The second section focuses on the tripartition of the spiritual life within the frame of the East Syriac ascetical tradition, in particular in reference to John the Solitary, “the father of the East Syriac spirituality”. And in consequence, the third chapter connects the three-fold stages of spiritual itinerary with the monastic life, for Joseph Hazzaya was a prominent representative of this milieu and all his writings were generated in this vein. The scope of this paper is to recuperate the personality of a great mystical author banished by the ‘Western’ Byzantine Church because of his belonging, as well as occasionally, by his own community.

data.title: Argumentative Strategies in Philoxenos of Mabbug’s Correspondence: From the Syriac Model to the Greek Model
data.abstractNote: The shift in argumentative strategies utilized by Philoxenos in his polemical correspondence over the nearly forty years of his ecclesiastical career reveals an adaptation of his literary practice to the model of legitimation found in Greek Christological polemics. Four phases are identified here based on chronology and style. Over time Philoxenos moved from a disputational approach relying on scriptural arguments and the Syriac literary tradition of Ephrem to an emphasis on historical precedent and the orthodox pedigree of the Miaphysite tradition and finally to a more pragmatic strategy for the success of the Miaphysite Christology within the Imperial Church.

data.title: The Fields, Flocks, and Finances of Monks: Economic Life at Nestorian Monasteries, 500-850
data.abstractNote: Nestorian Monasteries of the East Syrian Orient are considered to be important economic institutions in late Sasanian and early Islamic times. Syriac and Arabic sources, including church and monastic histories, saints' lives, liturgies, synod rulings, and the letters of Church officials are used to describe economic life at Nestorian monasteries. These institutions are shown to provide examples of Nestorian commercial enterprise and communal ownership. It is demonstrated that Nestorian monasteries were actively involved in the production, exchange, and appropriation of wealth in the forms of cash, land, flocks, and precious objects, and occupied a central position within urban and rural economic networks. It is argued that Nestorian monasticism was pervaded by attitudes which called for the renunciation of personal wealth and luxurious living. However, these views did not negate the importance of communal economic assets and activities, but were balanced by the  recognition of the need for monasteries to secure adequate economic resources for sustenance, and provision of charity to the needy. Beth 'Abhe is given special attention as a wealthy, powerful monastery in Sasanian and Islamic Iraq. Drawing upon information from The Book of Governors, written by Thomas of Marga in 840, Beth 'Abhe's economic prosperity is explained as a consequence of its relations with rich Persian Christian patrons, and effective economic management.

data.title: Ammonius d’Alexandrie et le Traité sur l’astrolabe de Sévère Sebokht
data.abstractNote: This contribution presents the text and translation of an unpublished part of the Syriac Treatise on the Astrolabe by Severus Sebokht recently found in a manuscript of Mardin (Turkey). This supplement to the text contains an astronomical exercise applied to the year 523 AD. Thanks to this date and to a detailed analysis of the structure of the text, we are now able to date the Greek treatise used by Severus Sebokht, and to specify how this 7th century Syriac scholar integrated it into his composition. Unfortunately, the name of the Greek author is never given in our document; nevertheless a combination of external information points to Ammonius of Alexandria as to its author.

data.title: Pottery Production and Exchange in Late Antique Syria (Fourth–Eighth Century A.D.): A Study of Some Imported and Local Wares
data.abstractNote: This paper will examine regional and extra-regional trade through the study of the distribution of some categories of ceramics in Syria. It will present a review based on a selection of local and imported wares, from publications, as well as personal observations, including fabric analyses. From the 4th c. A.D. onwards all fine wares were imported. Two major Syrian classes were produced: ‘Brittle Ware’ (Syrian cooking ware) and ‘North Syrian Amphorae’. The distribution of the different vessel categories illustrates a clear distinction between the coast and the hinterland. It also reveals active regional trade, using both fluvial and terrestrial means of transport.

data.title: Le Gannat Bussame
data.abstractNote: "Le "Gannat Bussame" ou "Jardin des Délices" est un volumineux commentaire des leçons de l'Ancien et du Nouveau Testament de toute l'année liturgique des Nestoriens. Ce n'est pas un ouvrage original, mais une espèce de "Catena Patrum"; l'auteur y a recueilli les interprétations des Docteurs anciens, nommés en général explicitement et cités mot à mot au long et au large à propos des différents livres de la Bible. Or beaucoup de ces ouvrages sont perdus aujourd'hui, et nous n'avons que des idées très générales et imparfaites sur l'ancienne exégèse orientale syriaque, qui dérive de l'école d'Antioche. Le Gannat Bussame sera donc une source précieuse pour l'étude de l'exégèse ancienne, c'est un document unique. Dès maintenant nous tenons à dire, que c'est une source inépuisable pour l'étude de Théodore de Mopsueste; il y a la part du lion même quand il n'est pas nommé; et en tout cas partout c'est l'esprit du Mephasqana, la première autorité biblique chez les Nestoriens qu'il n'était pas permis de contredire. [...] L'exégèse des prophètes est littérale et historique; telle identification fait songer aux hypothèses de la critique moderne." Les manuscrits; Les auteurs cités; L'auteur du Gannat Bussame; L'année liturgique et ses leçons bibliques d'après le Gannat Bussame; L'exégèse du Nouveau Testament dans le Gannat Bussame; Iso'dad et Gannat sur les évangiles; Iso'dad et Gannat sur les Actes; Iso'dad et Gannat sur les épîtres de saint Paul; Syriaque corrigeant le latin; Les commentaires sur les grandes épîtres de saint Paul.
